title: Snapshot Array
statement:
Design a class `SnapshotArray` that behaves like a fixed-size array of integers which can be saved and later read back as it was at each save.

- `SnapshotArray(length)` creates the array with `length` positions, all holding `0`.
- `set(index, val)` stores `val` at position `index`.
- `snap()` records the array's current contents and returns this save's id. Ids count up from `0`: the first call returns `0`, the second `1`, and so on.
- `get(index, snap_id)` returns the value position `index` held when the save with id `snap_id` was made. `snap_id` always refers to a save that has already happened.
constraints: 0 <= snap_id < number of snap() calls made so far
At most 5 * 10^4 calls in total are made to set, snap and get
notes:
## Intuition

Copying the whole array on every `snap()` is simple but costs O(length) per save. Most positions change rarely, so record only the changes: for each position keep a list of `[snapId, value]` pairs, where `snapId` is the save that the change will first appear in. These lists are naturally sorted by `snapId`, so reading a position at an old save is a binary search for the last change made before that save.

## Approach

1. Give every position a list `history[index]` that starts with `[-1, 0]`: the value is 0 before any save. Set `snapId = 0`, the id the next save will get.
2. `set(index, val)`: if the last record already belongs to `snapId`, overwrite its value; otherwise append `[snapId, val]`. Only the final value before a save matters.
3. `snap()`: increase `snapId` and return the previous value.
4. `get(index, snap_id)`: binary search the list for the last record whose id is at most `snap_id` and return its value. The `[-1, 0]` record guarantees one exists.

## Example 1, step by step

`SnapshotArray(3)` gives each position `[[-1, 0]]` and `snapId = 0`. `set(0, 5)` appends `[0, 5]` to position 0. `snap()` returns 0 and moves `snapId` to 1. `set(0, 6)` appends `[1, 6]`, so position 0 holds `[[-1, 0], [0, 5], [1, 6]]`. `get(0, 0)` searches for the last id at most 0, finds `[0, 5]` and returns `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) for `set` and `snap`, O(log k) for `get`, where k is the number of records at that position.
- Space: O(length + number of `set` calls).

## Pitfalls

- Several `set` calls between two saves must not pile up records with the same id; overwrite instead.
- The value written by `set` belongs to the next save, not the last one, so tag it with the current `snapId` before it is incremented.
- A position never set must still read as 0 for every save; the sentinel record handles it.
- The binary search must take the last record not after `snap_id`, so round `mid` up to avoid an endless loop.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `history` | per position, the list of `[snapId, value]` changes in order |
| `snapId` | id the next `snap()` will return; changes made now belong to it |
| `records` | the list for the position being read or written |
| `last` | the newest record of that position |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary search bounds and midpoint over `records` |
